projects.title: Why Do Some Shoppers Buy — and Most Just Look?
projects.cardDescription: Diagnosed why visitors leave without buying using 110M+ clickstream events from a real multi-category store — and found the leak is almost entirely upstream of checkout.
projects.impactStat: 0.92 ROC-AUC purchase model, holding at 0.946 a month later with no retraining
projects.oneSentenceDescription: A full-funnel behavioural diagnosis showing that once an item is carted it's bought 82.67% of the time — so the real leak, and the real opportunity, is at view → cart.
projects.summaryImpact: Across 42.4M October + 67.4M November 2019 clickstream events from a real multi-category online store, I diagnosed why visitors leave without buying — and where product, CX, and marketing teams can intervene. The data says this is a discovery problem, not a checkout problem: once an item is carted, it's bought 82.67% of the time. The leak is almost entirely upstream, at view → cart. Method: chunked pandas EDA on files too large for memory, session-level feature engineering across 9.2M October sessions, a LightGBM purchase-prediction model with SHAP, K-Means/decision-tree customer segmentation, and out-of-time validation on November.
projects.problemSpace: View volume is already enormous — 96% of all events are views. At this stage of the funnel, the business doesn't need more traffic; it needs more of the traffic it already has to convert. That reframes this from a marketing-acquisition problem into a full-funnel behavioural diagnosis. Scope spans two full months — October and November — specifically so seasonal noise (Black Friday) can be separated from durable behaviour. Every finding is tied to a named owner and a concrete action: Product Manager (owns the funnel and checkout experience), Customer Experience (owns on-site friction), and Marketing (owns acquisition, segments and promotions).

inputs.primarySource: REES46-style multi-category e-commerce clickstream (2019-Oct.csv, 2019-Nov.csv), joined against product catalogue and session data
inputs.size: 42.4M rows (Oct, 5.6GB) + 67.4M rows (Nov, 9GB); 3,022,234 distinct users; 166,794 distinct products; 3,444 brands; 126 category codes
inputs.collectionMethod: Full population log, not a sample
inputs.keyPredictors: Cart count, session duration, view count, n_unique_brands

projects.discovery: A 2.4x swing in purchase rate across hours of the day (0.96% at midnight vs 2.35% at 9am UTC) — a bigger lever than day-of-week. electronics.smartphone drives 27.1% of traffic but 45.5% of purchases, converting at 1.7x the average; Samsung, Apple, and Xiaomi make up ~50% of all purchases. Carted items average $187 but purchased items average $170 — a mild but consistent price-sensitivity signal right before checkout. Data quality was handled transparently: 0.07% exact duplicates removed; category_code missing on 31.8% of rows and brand on 14.4% (both optional upstream fields, not defects); product_id isn't a fully stable key (0.11% of products show more than one brand). Dead ends: dropped a per-session n_unique_products feature (~200k distinct values, expensive to compute, little signal over view count); rejected the highest-silhouette clustering result (k=2) because it was just a trivial one-time-vs-repeat-visitor split with no business use.
projects.execution: Built to survive files that don't fit in memory: 42.4M/67.4M-row files processed in 2M-row chunks with incremental aggregation; session-level grouping across 9.2M sessions took ~27 min/month due to near-UUID cardinality on user_session. Chose a LightGBM binary classifier (is_unbalance=True for the 6.8% positive rate, early stopping on validation AUC) over logistic regression because features interact non-linearly and LightGBM handles day-of-week natively. Leakage discipline: excluded user_session/user_id, literal purchase count, and n_events (which indirectly encodes purchase count). Avoided the classic evaluation trap where predict_proba ≥ 0.5 classifies everything as "no purchase" (93% accurate, useless) by picking an F1-optimal threshold from the precision-recall curve and reporting ROC-AUC/PR-AUC as the primary metrics. Segmentation used K-Means (k=6, chosen by silhouette among k=3–7) plus a shallow decision tree as a human-readable cross-check, both trained on behavioural features only with purchase outcome held out entirely. Validated by scoring the Oct-trained model on unseen Nov sessions with the exact same fixed threshold — a direct test of whether October alone was enough to build on.
projects.results: Full model ROC-AUC of 0.923, dropping to 0.697 without cart/session-duration features — most raw predictive power is session intensity, not behaviour type. SHAP shows more page views push toward purchase, while browsing more distinct brands and a higher max price viewed push slightly away from it — comparison shopping predicts against conversion. The Oct-trained model generalized to Nov without retraining (AUC 0.923 → 0.946). Six behavioural segments span a 146x range in purchase rate: 550,599 frequent repeat shoppers convert at 32.2% versus 572,589 bounce visitors at 0.2% — built from behaviour alone, with purchase outcome held out of clustering entirely.
projects.recommendations: Product/CX: reduce brand-comparison friction with clearer comparison tools and stronger recommendation ranking, since comparison-shoppers convert worse than focused browsers. Marketing: retarget the "long single-visit browser" segment — 946k users, ~57 min average session, only 13.2% convert — an already-warm audience that just doesn't return. Product: invest in discovery/recommendation surfaces rather than checkout UX, since cart→purchase is already 82.67% (a low ceiling) while view→cart has the highest possible upside. Limitations: category_code/brand have real missingness (31.8%/14.4%); product_id isn't a fully reliable brand key; no demographic or purchase-history features were available, only within-session behaviour. Next steps: A/B test the brand-comparison-friction hypothesis, build the live monitoring dashboard as a separate deliverable, and extend the model with a Nov-trained or combined Oct+Nov version if drift continues to widen.
